title: distinguish total distance (path length) from displacement (signed net change in position) when a position function reve
stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with position x(t) = t³ − 12t² + 36t, where x is in meters and t is in seconds. Over the interval from t = 0 to t = 7 s, which choice gives the total distance traveled and the displacement?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Distance is the total path length, which adds up every leg of the trip including the legs where the particle moves back. Taking the magnitude of the net displacement only gives the straight-line gap between start and end.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: v = 3at² + 2bt + c = 0 gives turning points t = 2, 6 s. Positions at t = 0, 2, 6, 7: x = 0, 32, 0, 7 m. Legs = 32, 32, 7 m, distance = 71 m. Displacement = 7 − 0 = 7 m. Without last leg: 71 − 7 = 64 m.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Displacement is the signed net change in position x(T) − x(0), not the path length. It equals the distance only when the particle never reverses direction, and here the velocity changes sign inside the interval.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The path length must include the final leg after the last turning point. Stopping the sum at the last time v = 0 leaves out the distance covered in the last stretch of the interval.

title: compute signed average acceleration through a rebound where velocity changes sign, avoiding speed-difference and reverse
stem: A ball travels along a straight line toward a wall. Take the x-axis to point toward the wall, so the ball's velocity just before impact is +8 m/s. It rebounds with a velocity of 6 m/s directly away from the wall, and contact lasts 0.020 s. Which choice gives the ball's average acceleration during contact, on the same x-axis?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Average acceleration is (final velocity − initial velocity)/Δt. Subtracting in the other order, initial minus final, flips the sign and describes the opposite direction of the velocity change.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The velocity reverses, so the signed change in velocity is the sum of the two speeds, not their difference. Using initial speed minus final speed treats the signed velocities as if both pointed the same way.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses final speed minus initial speed, which ignores that the velocity changes sign. The change in velocity runs from one sign to the other, so its magnitude is the sum of the two speeds.

title: use the relative signs of velocity and acceleration, obtained by differentiating, to decide speeding up or slowing down
stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity v(t) = t² − 6t + 8, in SI units. At t = 1.0 s, which choice correctly gives its acceleration and whether it is speeding up or slowing down?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The acceleration value is right, but the verdict is reversed. An object speeds up when its velocity and acceleration have the same sign and slows down when they have opposite signs, so the sign of acceleration alone does not decide it.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This reverses the sign of the derivative and then judges consistently from the wrong sign. The acceleration is the slope dv/dt evaluated at the given time, and its sign must be compared with the sign of the velocity there.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: v = 3 m/s, a = −4 m/s²; v·a = −12 so slowing down. dv/dt = 2t − 6 → at t = 1: −4; v(1) = 1 − 6 + 8 = 3. Wrong slip value = −5.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Differentiating t² gives 2t, not t. Using a = t − 6 drops the factor of 2 from the power rule, which gives the wrong magnitude of the acceleration.

title: recognize that average velocity is displacement over time (area under v-t) and not the endpoint average or midpoint valu
stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity v(t) = 3t², in SI units. What is its average velocity over the interval from t = 0 to t = 4.0 s?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: ∫v dt from 0 to 4 = 64 m; average = 64/4 = 16 m/s. Endpoint average = (0 + 48)/2 = 24; v at midpoint (2 s) = 12; v(4) = 48.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Averaging the initial and final velocities is valid only when acceleration is constant. Here a = dv/dt changes with time, so the velocity graph is curved and this overestimates or misstates the time-average.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The velocity at the midpoint time is not the average velocity for a curved v(t). The average velocity is the displacement, the area under the curve, divided by the elapsed time.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is the instantaneous velocity at the end of the interval. Average velocity is the displacement divided by the time, which uses the area under the whole v(t) curve.

title: find final position from a velocity-time graph as initial position plus signed area, with segments below the axis counte
stem: The velocity of a cart on a straight track is described by straight-line segments joining these (t, v) points: (0 s, 0 m/s), (2 s, +6 m/s), (5 s, +6 m/s), (8 s, −4 m/s). The cart is at x = −3 m at t = 0. What is its position at t = 8 s?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Position change is the signed area under the v-t graph, so area below the t-axis must be subtracted. Adding every area as positive gives the total path length, not the net displacement.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: Signed area = 6 + 18 + 3 = 27 m; x = −3 + 27 = +24 m. Absolute-area version: 31.8 + −3 = +28.8. Final velocity = −4.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The area under the graph gives only the displacement, the change in position. The initial position must be added to find where the cart is at the end.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This reads the final velocity as if it were the position. The v-t graph shows velocity, so the position comes from the accumulated area under it plus the starting position.

title: locate maximum velocity where acceleration is zero and compute it by integrating a(t) plus the initial velocity
stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with acceleration a(t) = 6 − 2t, in SI units, for t ≥ 0. Its velocity at t = 0 is −2 m/s. What is the greatest velocity the particle reaches for t ≥ 0?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The initial velocity is part of the total. Velocity at any time is the initial velocity plus the area under the a-t curve, so leaving v(0) out gives the change in velocity, not the velocity itself.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: v(t) = −2 + 6t − 1t². a = 0 at t = 6/2 = 3 s. v = −2 + 18 − 9 = 7 m/s. Without v0: 9; max a = 6; constant-a: −2 + 6·3 = 16.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This reads the peak of the acceleration curve as the peak velocity. The velocity is greatest when the acceleration is zero, and its value comes from integrating a(t), not from the maximum of a(t).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This applies v = v₀ + at with the initial acceleration for the whole time. The acceleration is not constant, since a decreases linearly with time, so the area under the a-t curve is a triangle, not a rectangle.

title: resolve a river-crossing problem into independent perpendicular motions in the ground frame: crossing time from the boat
stem: A river is 120 m wide and flows east at 3 m/s relative to the banks. A boat has a speed of 4 m/s relative to the water, and its heading is kept pointed directly north, perpendicular to the banks. Which choice gives the crossing time and the downstream drift when it reaches the far bank?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crossing time 30 s; downstream drift 90 m.
choices.rationale: Correct: Heading straight across: t = W/u = 120/4 = 30 s; drift = w·t = 3·30 = 90 m. Resultant speed 5: t = 24, drift = 72. Swapped: t = 40, drift = 160. Boat speed × t = 120.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crossing time 24 s; downstream drift 72 m.
choices.rationale: The boat's speed relative to the water, not the resultant speed relative to the bank, sets the crossing time, because only the boat's heading component across the river carries it across. Using the resultant speed over the width is too fast.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Crossing time 40 s; downstream drift 160 m.
choices.rationale: This swaps the roles of the speeds. The crossing time is the river width divided by the boat's speed across the river, and the drift is the current speed multiplied by that time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Crossing time 30 s; downstream drift 120 m.
choices.rationale: The crossing time is right, but the drift is found with the boat's speed instead of the current's. The sideways drift comes from the current carrying the boat downstream during the crossing.

title: solve two-dimensional projectile motion launched from a height with a quadratic for the time of flight, using separate h
stem: A ball is launched from the top of a 20 m cliff with a speed of 25 m/s at 37° above the horizontal (take sin 37° = 0.60 and cos 37° = 0.80). Neglect air resistance and use g = 10 m/s². How far from the base of the cliff, horizontally, does the ball land on the level ground below?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses the flight time for a launch and landing at the same height. The landing point is lower than the launch point, so the ball stays in the air longer and travels farther.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: Taking up as positive, y: h + vy·t − 5t² = 0 with h = 20, vy = 15; t = 4 s. Range = 20·4 = 80 m. Free-fall time √(2h/g) = 2 s → 40 m. Flat-ground time = 2·15/10 = 3 s → 60 m. Launch speed 25·t = 100 m.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses only the time to fall the height h from rest. The ball first rises, so its vertical motion starts with an upward velocity and the total time is longer than a drop from rest.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The horizontal distance is the horizontal velocity component times time, not the launch speed times time. The launch speed includes the vertical component, which does not move the ball horizontally.

title: obtain speed as the magnitude of the velocity vector found by differentiating each position component, not from |r|, com
stem: A particle moves in the xy-plane with position components x(t) = 2t² and y(t) = 3t, in meters with t in seconds. What is the particle's speed at t = 2.0 s?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the rate of change of the particle's distance from the origin, d|r|/dt. Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, |v|, and the two agree only when the motion is directly away from the origin.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Adding the velocity components is not the speed. Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, found from the square root of the sum of the squares of its components.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is the magnitude of the position vector divided by time, an average-like quantity from the origin. Speed at an instant is the magnitude of dr/dt evaluated at that time, not |r|/t.
